plan.note: What players who finished on this comp had on their board at the end of each stage (units in 30 %+ of their games). The API starts at the end of stage 3, when most players are already level 7 or 8, so the opener is the 1 and 2 costs they were still holding then: the units to pick up in stages 1 and 2. Green ring = new at that step, faded = not on the next step's board. Lv = the most common player level at that point. Items are the ones the unit ends the game with (the API gives none per stage).

gamePlan.title: Game plan
gamePlan.description: Which Pokémon to field early, mid and late game in Kanto Tactics Ranked: presence at the end of stages 3 and 4 and on the final board of the comps that finish well, and whether they stay until the end.
gamePlan.subtitle: what the good comps field at each point of the game
gamePlan.intro: The API only scores the end of the game, so there is no “best early comp”. What it does publish is the board of the players who finished on a good comp at the end of stages 3 and 4 ({guided} reliable comps), when they are already level 7 or 8. Opener keeps only the 1 and 2 costs of those stage 3 boards: the units worth picking up in stages 1 and 2, and the comps they lead to. The other tabs show the whole board at each point and whether a unit stays until the end. Click a unit for the final comps that field it there; every comp page has its own Opener → Stage 3 → Stage 4 → Final plan.

about.title: About the data
about.description: Where the numbers come from, how tiers are computed, and what the Kanto Tactics Meta API does and does not publish.
about.sourceText: Everything comes from the game's public <api>Meta API</api>: Ranked games, humans only, over the last 7 days across every rules version in the window ({from} to {to}). The API regenerates daily at 03:40 UTC and this site is rebuilt from that run every morning, so every page is a static copy of the day's data.
about.tiersText1: Pokémon, items and types use the game's own tiers: average place against the week's reference place ({ref}), S ≤ {s}, A ≤ {a}, B ≤ {b}. The API stops at C; D is this site's split, mirroring S: average place at or above {d}. A Pokémon's tier counts every board it ends on, in any comp, so a unit can be B on its own and still sit in most tier S comps; its page says in how many.
about.tiersText2: Comps are graded stricter, on the pessimistic average (avg + 95 % CI): S ≤ {s}, A ≤ {a}, B ≤ {b}, C ≤ {c}, D above. The “Best” sort uses the same number, so a comp with 11 games and a ± 0.9 interval cannot sit above a steady one. Comps under {minNe} effective games only have their 4 core units in the API (no stars, shares or board) and are hidden unless you include them.
about.rolesText: Items are split by the stat they give: offensive (Attack, Sp. Atk, attack speed, crit, Energy, drain) or defensive (HP, Defense, Sp. Def, shields). The carry is the unit that collects the most offensive item share, the sub the second one when it is geared at least 40 % as often, the tank the unit with the most defensive items. Any other unit whose most common item sits on it in 20 %+ of games shows its gear in the list rows too.
about.missing: What the API does not give
about.missingText: No pick rate or result for Seals (the Seals tab is a catalogue). No board for comps under 50 boards: the site then shows where each unit usually stands in the comps that do have one. New units of rules v{rules} that the game data file (v{data}) does not describe yet get their cost and type from the game changelog and the standard sprite. If the API stops answering, the site keeps its last build and says so.
